subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which two substances are the raw materials (reactants) for photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Plants take in carbon dioxide and water and use light energy to convert them into glucose and oxygen.

questions.q: What are the products of photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Photosynthesis produces glucose (a store of energy) and oxygen, which is released as a by-product.

questions.q: In which part of a plant cell does photosynthesis take place?
questions.explain: Chloroplasts contain the green pigment chlorophyll, which absorbs the light energy needed for photosynthesis.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the energy change during photosynthesis?
options: It takes in light energy, so it is endothermic
It releases heat energy, so it is exothermic
It neither takes in nor releases energy
It only releases heat to the surroundings
questions.explain: Photosynthesis transfers light energy into chemical energy in glucose, so it takes in energy and is endothermic.

questions.q: Which is the correct balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Six carbon dioxide and six water molecules produce one glucose molecule and six oxygen molecules.

questions.q: What is the role of chlorophyll in photosynthesis?
options: It absorbs light energy for photosynthesis
It transports water through the leaf
It releases oxygen directly into the air
questions.explain: Chlorophyll is the green pigment that absorbs light energy so it can be used to make glucose.

questions.q: A leaf is tested with iodine solution and turns blue-black. What does this show?
questions.explain: Iodine solution turns blue-black in the presence of starch, showing photosynthesis has occurred and glucose has been stored as starch.

questions.q: Which of the following is a limiting factor of photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide concentration, light intensity and temperature are the three limiting factors of photosynthesis.

questions.q: What is meant by a 'limiting factor' of photosynthesis?
options: A factor that, when in short supply, restricts the rate of photosynthesis
A factor that always increases the rate of photosynthesis
A mineral ion needed to make chlorophyll
A waste product removed during photosynthesis
questions.explain: A limiting factor is the one in shortest supply that holds back the rate of photosynthesis at that moment.

questions.q: On a graph of rate of photosynthesis against light intensity, the line levels off and stays flat at high light intensity. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Another factor, such as carbon dioxide or temperature, is now limiting
Light intensity is the only factor affecting the rate
Chlorophyll has been destroyed by the bright light
questions.explain: Once light is no longer limiting, the rate is capped by another factor like carbon dioxide concentration or temperature.

questions.q: Above the optimum temperature, the rate of photosynthesis falls sharply. Why?
options: There is suddenly too much carbon dioxide
Light can no longer reach the leaf
The leaf runs out of chlorophyll
questions.explain: High temperatures denature the enzymes that control photosynthesis, so the reactions slow down or stop.

questions.q: A grower wants to increase the rate of photosynthesis in a greenhouse on a warm, bright day. Which change would be most effective?
options: Removing all minerals from the soil
questions.explain: When light and temperature are already high, carbon dioxide is likely to be limiting, so adding more raises the rate.

questions.q: Which leaf tissue contains the most chloroplasts and is the main site of photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Palisade mesophyll cells are packed with chloroplasts near the top of the leaf where most light is absorbed.

questions.q: A variegated (green and white) leaf is destarched, left in the light, then tested with iodine. Which part turns blue-black?
questions.explain: Only the green parts contain chlorophyll, so only they can photosynthesise and make starch that turns iodine blue-black.

questions.q: Why are most leaves broad and thin?
options: To give a large surface area and a short diffusion distance
To store large amounts of starch and water
To reduce the amount of light they absorb
To stop gases from entering or leaving
questions.explain: A broad, thin shape captures plenty of light and lets gases diffuse in and out over short distances.

questions.q: What controls the opening and closing of the stomata?
questions.explain: Guard cells surround each stoma and change shape to open or close the pore, controlling gas exchange and water loss.

questions.q: What is the main function of the waxy cuticle on a leaf?
options: To reduce water loss from the leaf surface
To allow gases to diffuse more quickly
To transport sugars around the plant
questions.explain: The waterproof waxy cuticle helps to reduce evaporation of water from the upper surface of the leaf.

questions.q: Which mineral ion is needed by plants to make chlorophyll?
questions.explain: Magnesium ions are required to produce chlorophyll, so a shortage causes yellowing of the leaves.

questions.q: Nitrate ions are needed by plants mainly to make which substance?
questions.explain: Nitrate ions supply the nitrogen plants use to build amino acids and therefore proteins for growth.

questions.q: A plant shows yellowing between the veins of its leaves (chlorosis) but is otherwise growing. Which mineral is most likely deficient?
questions.explain: Yellowing caused by a lack of chlorophyll points to a magnesium deficiency, since magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll.
